meta.title: Advanced Relative Clauses
meta.description: Advanced English grammar topics themed around Music and Artists
meta.info: This test includes 30 questions focusing on combined C1-C2 level grammar structures, primarily featuring Advanced Relative Clauses paired with other complex topics like inversion, subjunctive mood, conditionals, and more.
meta.author: Qwen3.7

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronouns to complete the sentence.
data.question: The composer, to _____ the award was given, is the one without _____ the symphony would never have been completed.

explanation.text: This combines advanced relative clauses with prepositions. 'To whom' is the correct object form after the preposition 'to', and 'without whom' is the correct object form after the preposition 'without'.
explanation.concept: Preposition + relative pronoun (whom)
explanation.formula: Preposition + whom (for people)
examples: The artist, to whom I spoke, is the one without whom the project would fail.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines an advanced non-defining relative clause with the mandative subjunctive. 'Album' is singular, requiring 'has been'. After 'demanded that', the subjunctive requires the base form 'release'.
explanation.concept: Subject-verb agreement in relative clauses and mandative subjunctive
explanation.formula: Noun, whose + singular noun + has/have + past participle, demanded that + subject + base verb
examples: The director, whose film has been praised, demanded that the studio release it.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The song, _____ by a famous producer, _____ a global hit within weeks of its release.

explanation.text: This combines a reduced relative clause (past participle 'produced' for passive meaning) with a main clause in the past simple tense ('became').
explanation.concept: Reduced passive relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, + past participle + , + subject + past simple verb
examples: The book, written by a novice, became a bestseller.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

multiErrorSegments.text: The band, all of whose members

explanation.text: This combines advanced relative clauses with quantifiers and subject-verb agreement. 'Members' is plural, requiring 'are'. 'Each' is singular, requiring 'has'.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Quantifiers + Subject-Verb Agreement
explanation.concept: Agreement with quantifiers in relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, all of whose + plural noun + plural verb; each of which + singular verb
examples: The team, all of whose players are professionals, has won, each of whom has a trophy.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronouns to complete the sentence.
data.question: The venue, in _____ the concert was held, must have been the one _____ acoustics are legendary.

explanation.text: This combines a preposition + relative pronoun ('in which') with a possessive relative pronoun ('whose') referring to a thing (the venue's acoustics). 'Must have been' is a modal of deduction.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Modal Verbs of Deduction
explanation.concept: Preposition + which and possessive whose for things
explanation.formula: Noun, in which + clause, must have been + noun + whose + noun + verb
examples: The building, in which they met, must have been the one whose doors were locked.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a cleft sentence with an embedded relative clause. 'Conductor' is a person, requiring 'who' (not 'which'). 'Critics' is plural, requiring the plural verb 'praise'.
explanation.concept: Relative pronouns for people and subject-verb agreement in clefts
explanation.formula: It is + person + who + verb + object + who/whom + plural subject + plural verb
examples: It is the teacher who inspires the students whom the parents praise.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the elliptical relative clause.
data.question: The musician _____ playing the cello, _____ a master of the instrument, received a standing ovation.

explanation.text: This combines an elliptical relative clause ('who was' can be reduced, but 'who was' is the full form) with a participle clause ('being') for additional description.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Ellipsis + Participle Clauses
explanation.concept: Ellipsis in relative clauses and present participle phrases
explanation.formula: Noun + who + was/were + verb-ing, + being + noun phrase, + main verb
examples: The artist who was painting the mural, being a local hero, received applause.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with verb patterns. The verb 'avoid' must be followed by a gerund ('performing'), not a to-infinitive.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Gerunds vs. Infinitives
explanation.concept: Verb patterns following relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who + is known + to-infinitive, avoids + verb-ing
examples: The chef, who is known to cook well, avoids using salt.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The more complex the composition, _____ the musician, _____ reputation precedes him, finds it to play.

explanation.text: This combines a double comparative structure with a non-defining relative clause using the possessive relative pronoun 'whose'.
explanation.concept: Double comparatives and possessive relative pronouns
explanation.formula: The + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + subject, whose + noun + verb, + finds it + to-infinitive
examples: The harder the task, the more the leader, whose skills are vast, enjoys it.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines non-defining relative clauses with discourse markers. 'However' is the correct contrastive marker here, not 'therefore', which indicates a result.
explanation.concept: Contrastive discourse markers in relative clause structures
explanation.formula: Noun, which + was + adjective, however, + verb + to-infinitive, which + is + noun
examples: The event, which was planned carefully, however, failed, which is unfortunate.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronoun and conditional structure.
data.question: The artist, _____ latest work revolutionized the genre, would have won the Grammy had it not been for the controversy.

explanation.text: This combines a possessive relative clause ('whose latest work') with a third conditional inversion ('had it not been').
explanation.concept: Possessive relative pronouns and inverted conditionals
explanation.formula: Noun, whose + noun + verb, would have + past participle + had + subject + not + past participle
examples: The inventor, whose device changed the world, would have been richer had he not sold the patent.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines advanced relative clauses with subject-verb agreement rules. 'A number of' takes a plural verb ('were', 'have'), while 'the number of' takes a singular verb ('is').
explanation.concept: Agreement with 'a number of' vs. 'the number of'
explanation.formula: A number of + plural noun, which + plural verb + have + past participle; the number of + plural noun + singular verb
examples: A number of the books, which were written by her, have sold, while the number of copies is low.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: By next year, the orchestra, which _____ together for a decade, will have performed this symphony over fifty times.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with the present perfect continuous tense to show an action continuing up to a future point, paired with the future perfect in the main clause.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Future Perfect + Present Perfect Continuous
explanation.concept: Ongoing action in a relative clause leading to a future perfect main clause
explanation.formula: By + future time, noun, which + has/have been + verb-ing, will have + past participle
examples: By tomorrow, the team, which has been training for months, will have finished the project.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with a mixed conditional. The relative pronoun 'who' acts as the subject of the conditional, so the second 'he' is redundant and must be removed.
explanation.concept: Embedding conditionals within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who, if + subject + had + past participle, would + be + verb-ing, + main verb
examples: The student, who, if she had studied, would be passing now, is retaking the exam.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The composer, who _____ to have written the manuscript in the 18th century, is considered a genius.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with an advanced passive reporting structure ('is believed to have written').
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Advanced Passive Structures
explanation.concept: Passive reporting verbs in relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who + is/are + believed/said/thought + to have + past participle
examples: The inventor, who is said to have created the device, is famous.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with 'not only... but also' inversion. When 'not only' begins the relative clause, it triggers subject-auxiliary inversion, but since the relative pronoun 'who' is the subject, it becomes 'who not only sings'.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Not Only ... But Also
explanation.concept: Correlative conjunctions within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who + not only + verb, but + also + verb
examples: The manager, who not only leads the team but also mentors them, is respected.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The manager, _____ decisions the band resents, is someone it is high time they _____.

explanation.text: This combines a possessive relative clause ('whose decisions') with the 'it's high time' structure, which requires the past subjunctive ('replaced').
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + It's High Time
explanation.concept: Possessive relative pronouns and past subjunctive for urgency
explanation.formula: Noun, whose + noun + subject + verb, is someone + it is high time + subject + past simple
examples: The policy, whose effects we hate, is one it is high time we changed.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with 'as though' + past subjunctive ('were') to describe an unreal or hypothetical present situation.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + As Though / As If
explanation.concept: Unreal comparisons within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who + verb + as though + subject + past subjunctive (were)
examples: The child, who acts as though he were an adult, is very mature.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the inverted relative clause.
data.question: The musician, _____ talented was he that he mastered the violin in a year, is now a teacher.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with 'so + adjective' inversion ('so talented was he') for emphasis.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + So / Such Inversion
explanation.concept: Emphatic inversion within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, so + adjective + be + subject + that + clause
examples: The storm, so fierce was it that it destroyed the roof, is remembered.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with negative adverbial inversion. The phrase 'under no circumstances' must follow the relative pronoun and trigger inversion ('should under no circumstances be').
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Negative Adverbial Inversion
explanation.concept: Negative inversion within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who + should + under no circumstances + be + past participle
examples: The document, which should under no circumstances be leaked, is secure.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The sound engineer, _____ you need any assistance, is the one to _____ you must speak.

explanation.text: This combines a conditional inversion ('should you need') embedded as a relative clause modifier, with a preposition + relative pronoun ('to whom').
explanation.concept: Conditional inversion and preposition + whom
explanation.formula: Noun, should + subject + verb, is the one + preposition + whom + subject + verb
examples: The guide, should you need help, is the person to whom you should talk.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause structure with second conditional inversion. 'Were I' must be followed by the to-infinitive 'to choose', not the gerund 'choosing'.
explanation.concept: Inversion with 'were' for hypothetical situations
explanation.formula: Noun, were + subject + to + base verb, is the one + whose + noun + subject + verb
examples: The book, were I to pick one, is the one whose cover I like.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The singer, _____ three platinum albums, who is now retiring, will give a farewell concert.

explanation.text: This combines a perfect participle clause ('having released') indicating an action completed before the main verb, with a non-defining relative clause ('who is now retiring').
explanation.concept: Perfect participle clauses preceding relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, having + past participle + object, who + is/are + verb-ing, + will + verb
examples: The athlete, having won gold, who is now retiring, will give a speech.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with article usage. 'Unique' starts with a consonant sound (/j/), so it correctly takes the indefinite article 'a', not 'an'.
explanation.concept: Indefinite articles before consonant sounds in relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, which + is + a + word starting with /j/ sound
examples: The idea, which is a unique concept, has won awards.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronouns to complete the sentence.
data.question: The instrument, without _____ the melody would be incomplete, is the one to _____ the composer was most attached.

explanation.text: This combines two advanced relative clauses with prepositions. After a preposition ('without', 'to'), 'which' must be used for things, not 'that'.
explanation.concept: Preposition + which for inanimate objects
explanation.formula: Noun, without which + clause, is the one + to which + clause
examples: The tool, without which we cannot work, is the one to which we are accustomed.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with a noun clause acting as the subject. The subject 'What makes the artist... so compelling' is singular, requiring the singular verb 'is'.
explanation.concept: Subject-verb agreement with complex noun clause subjects
explanation.formula: What + makes + noun, who + clause, + singular verb + adjective
examples: What makes the book, which is long, interesting is the plot.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronoun and phrasal verb structure.
data.question: The producer, _____ the band looks up to, is the one who came up with the idea.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with a phrasal verb ('looks up to'). The relative pronoun is the object of the preposition 'to', requiring the objective case 'whom'.
explanation.concept: Relative pronouns as objects of prepositions in phrasal verbs
explanation.formula: Noun, whom + subject + phrasal verb (verb + preposition), is the one
examples: The mentor, whom we rely on, is the one who helps.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with 'if only' for past regret. The relative pronoun 'who' acts as the subject, so the second 'he' is redundant and must be removed.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Wish / If Only
explanation.concept: Embedding 'if only' within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, who, if only + subject + had + past participle, would + verb
examples: The player, who, if only he had trained, would have won, is retired.

data.hint: Choose the correct structures to complete the sentence.
data.question: The more famous the artist becomes, the more pressure, _____ is often underestimated, he faces.

explanation.text: This combines a double comparative structure with a non-defining relative clause. 'Which' is the correct relative pronoun for things ('pressure') in a non-defining clause.
explanation.concept: Non-defining relative clauses interrupting double comparatives
explanation.formula: The + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + noun, which + verb, + subject + verb
examples: The harder it rains, the more water, which is dangerous, we get.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines a non-defining relative clause with a mixed conditional inversion. The relative pronoun 'which' acts as the subject, so 'if it' and the second 'it' are redundant. The correct form is 'which, had it been promoted better, would be a hit today'.
explanation.topic: Advanced Relative Clauses + Mixed Conditionals + Passive
explanation.concept: Embedding inverted mixed conditionals within relative clauses
explanation.formula: Noun, which, had + subject + been + past participle, would + be + noun
examples: The project, which, had it been funded, would be successful, was canceled.
